title: Equilibration of generalized subsystems: a quantum-channel approach
authors: Pedro S. Correia, Adalberto D. Varizi, Gabriel Dias Carvalho
abstract: Quantum systems governed by unitary and reversible microscopic dynamics may nevertheless exhibit equilibration, in the sense that some effective description becomes time-independent. Standard equilibration results usually consider two separate situations: system-environment structures, in which the composite system evolves unitarily while the system of interest equilibrates, and restricted measurements, such as coarse-grained POVMs and observables, in which the measurement statistics equilibrate. Here, we bring these descriptions into a common state-level framework using the concept of generalized subsystems, where the accessible effective state appears as the output of a quantum channel acting on the microscopic state. We derive bounds showing that generalized subsystems equilibrate when their dimension is small compared with the effective dimension of the discarded microscopic information. We further show that this condition is met for typical initial states in large subspaces and that the resulting equilibrium description is largely insensitive to microscopic initial details. The framework recovers the usual equilibration bounds for ordinary subsystems and finite families of POVMs. As an example, we also introduce a finite-resolution energy channel that maps unresolved microscopic energy levels into effective energy levels, thereby making residual effective coherences explicit and showing how spectral multiplicities constrain those coherences while strengthening equilibration. Our results provide a unified state-level formulation of quantum equilibration under general forms of limited accessible information.
summary: This paper develops a unified theoretical framework to study quantum equilibration when information access is limited, modeling the accessible state via a quantum channel acting on the full system. The key finding is that equilibration bounds are determined by comparing the subsystem size to the effective dimension of discarded microscopic details. This has broad implications for understanding thermalization in realistic, measurement-constrained quantum systems.
main_problem: The core problem is understanding quantum equilibration—how an effective, time-independent description emerges for accessible degrees of freedom even when the underlying microscopic dynamics are unitary and reversible.
main_result: The authors provide a unified state-level framework showing that equilibration bounds depend on the ratio between the subsystem dimension and the effective dimension of discarded microscopic information. They also show that accessible coherences are strongly suppressed during this process.
method: The work introduces 'generalized subsystems,' modeling the accessible state as the output of a quantum channel acting on the full system state, allowing for a unified treatment encompassing partial traces and measurement restrictions (POVMs).
model_or_system: The analysis is general but uses the Ising spin chain model as a concrete example to test equilibration bounds. The dynamics are governed by unitary evolution under a Hamiltonian, and information access is restricted via quantum channels ($\Lambda$).
key_observables: Time-averaged trace distance $D(ho_S(t), \omega_S)$ (measuring deviation from equilibrium) and accessible coherence measures $C_{l1}(\varrho_S)$.
important_parameters: The ratio of the subsystem dimension ($d_S$) to the effective dimension explored by microscopic dynamics ($	ext{deff}(\Lambda_c[\omega])$).
main_assumptions: The framework assumes that restricted access can be modeled by a quantum channel (CPTP map), and some derivations rely on non-degenerate energy gaps for simplification.
figures_summary: Figure 2 illustrates the time evolution of both the trace distance $D(\varrho_S(t), \omega_S)$ and the accessible coherence $C_{l1}(\varrho_S(t))$ for a finite Ising chain, showing decay towards equilibrium/zero.
paper_structure: The paper develops the generalized quantum channel framework first, deriving sharp bounds based on effective dimensions. It then applies this to specific physical scenarios like POVMs and finite-resolution energy measurements, culminating in numerical simulations on an Ising model to demonstrate coherence suppression.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful, general mathematical tool for analyzing thermalization and relaxation in complex quantum systems where the environment or measurement process is not simply modeled by a partial trace. It unifies several distinct physical concepts under one rigorous framework.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Examples of limited accessible information. (a) In the standard subsystem picture, only a subset of particles is accessible, while the rest forms an inaccessible environment. (b) Finite-resolution energy measurements group microscopic energy levels into effective energy win- dows, so that only a coarse-grained energy description is accessible. (c) In a blurred and saturated detector, distinct microscopic configurations can become indistinguishable at the accessible level; for instance, two microscopic qubits may be described by a single effective two-level system.

FIG. 2. Numerical illustration of the finite-resolution energy channel for a finite Ising spin chain. In both panels, the initial state is a balanced coherent superposition of all energy eigenstates, and the spectrum is partitioned into K = N resolved energy windows. Left: temporal behavior of the trace distance D(ϱS(t), ωS), together with its time average and the two equilibration bounds shown in the inset. Right: temporal behavior of the accessible coherence Cl1(ϱS(t)) between distinct effective energy levels, included as a diagnostic of the off-diagonal sector already controlled by trace-distance equilibration; the inset shows the normalized average coherence ⟨Cl1(ϱS(t))⟩t/Cl1(ϱS(0)).
